# Survey notes: blaze / relax / wild

Date: 2026-11-14

To use in the design of zustc, I read three projects and organized the findings (I only read the source of main as of 2026-11-14 and did not build them. Only wild was actually used, by installing 0.10.0 from crates.io).

- blaze: https://github.com/indexable-inc/blaze
- relax: https://github.com/makepad/relax
- wild: https://github.com/wild-linker/wild

## Overview

| | blaze | relax | wild |
|---|---|---|---|
| What it is | A replacement for cargo. A resident daemon builds without using rustc | A Rust JIT and live compiler | A fast ELF linker |
| Frontend | A fork of rust-analyzer (rowan, hir-def/hir-ty). The trait solver is vendored from rustc | All its own (lexer, Pratt parser, typeck and next-solver ported from rustc). No dependency crates | - |
| IR | HIR → MIR → (CLIF / LIR) | typeck::Body → RIR (non-SSA vregs, CFG) | - |
| Backend | Currently MIR → CLIF. v2 plans copy-and-patch stencils for dev builds and LLVM for release builds, and will not use Cranelift for native code generation | Its own (interp → O1 → O3, linear scan regalloc) | - |
| Compilation unit | One monomorphized function instance | One function instance (lazily, on first call) | Input sections |
| Cache key | BLAKE3, with the body α-normalized and no spans. Callees by interface hash only | 128bit. compiler ID + instance + interface fingerprints of dependencies + body | - |
| Linking | Its own linker (about 89k lines). In-place patching and jump tables | No linker (JIT). Has a startup image | Parallel. `--gc-sections` is on by default, no ICF, LTO only via plugins |

## What can be copied from blaze

1. **Per-function cache + callees by interface hash only** (`crates/blaze-codegen/src/template.rs`).
   Compiled code holds callees by "position in the reference list", so editing a callee's body does not recompile the caller. Only the relocation names are reassigned.
   → zustc adopted this as-is (relocations in a `Blob` are held by function ID or name).
2. **No whitespace, comments or spans in the body hash** (`docs/v2/plan/design/item-hash.md`).
   blaze also α-normalizes local variables into de Bruijn-style indices, so renaming a local variable does not invalidate either.
   → zustc only goes as far as lexer-level normalization. No α-normalization yet.
3. **Reachability**: compile only what is reachable from main, tests and exports.
4. **Do ICF and polymorphization in the compiler, not the linker**:
   - Keys are made from layout (size/align/ABI), so `Vec<A>` and `Vec<B>` can share code.
   - Identical functions are folded by a hash of code + relocation targets (`dedupe.rs`).
   - Functions that differ only in constants are parameterized (`fold.rs`).
5. **In dev builds, make symbol names short hashes and keep only the line table**.
6. **Incremental linking**: leave slack in `.text`, append changed functions at the end, and call through a jump table. It is enough to consider this once linking dominates.
7. **What is not needed**: the daemon, DBSP, stencils. These are monorepo-scale mechanisms and overkill for personal use.

## What can be copied from relax

1. **Demand-driven**: both name resolution and type checking are done only for what is reached (`front/src/lazy.rs`, `demand.rs`). For AOT this becomes "compile only the set reachable from main".
2. **Cache format** (`compiler/src/cache.rs`, `store.rs`):
   - 1 crate = 1 file. After the header comes a sorted index, then an append-only payload. It switches between A/B index slots to be crash-safe.
   - Relocations are saved with stable IDs (definition keys, string bytes, and so on).
   - When inlining, it also records the keys of the inlined functions.
   → zustc also uses one file. Index + payload, decoding only on a hit.
3. **Its own small std** (about 120k lines). It does not compile rust-src, so both build time and binaries are smaller.
4. **Key points of the optimization tier** (1.12x vs LLVM):
   - Inlining (rustc's cost model).
   - SROA-style work on stack slots. Cranelift has no SROA, so this part has to be written by hand.
   - LICM, bounds check elimination via value range analysis.
5. **The parser has no error recovery and stops at the first error**. That is enough for personal use.

## What can be copied from wild / what zustc should do itself

1. **How to emit objects**:
   - Put each function in its own section (`ObjectBuilder::per_function_section(true)`). Without this, `--gc-sections` removes nothing.
   - Make non-exported things Local/hidden.
   - Use `-no-pie` to avoid emitting `R_*_RELATIVE`.
   - Put strings in `SHF_MERGE|SHF_STRINGS` sections. But merge sections are not GC'd, so do not put dead data in them.
2. **LTO is only via linker plugins (LLVM bitcode / GIMPLE)**. Cranelift has no matching IR, so wild is just a native linker.
   **Inlining, DCE, deduplication of monomorphizations and ICF can only be done whole-program in the compiler.**
   → zustc makes 1 program = 1 object and does DCE by reachability in the compiler.
3. **Do not go through the cc driver**:
   - Measured: cc + lld took 21ms; starting wild directly took 5ms.
   - With the `libwild` crate it can be called as a library, and the `FileSystem` trait lets objects be passed directly from memory. There is no need to write a `.o`.
4. **Incremental linking is wild's end goal, but it is not implemented yet**.
5. Implementation techniques:
   - mmap and borrow with `'data`, no copying.
   - Use dense `u32` IDs and Vec tables.
   - Compute name hashes once and reuse them.
   - Size the output first, then split it into disjoint `&mut` slices and write in parallel.
   - fork and move cleanup to the background.

## What zustc adopted (in priority order)

| Idea | Source | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Per-function machine code cache. Only callee signatures go into the key | blaze template / relax cache | Implemented |
| Item hash that ignores whitespace and comments (own lexer) | blaze item-hash | Implemented |
| Parse only changed items with syn (item summary cache) | relax demand / blaze early cutoff | Implemented |
| Reachability from main. Unreachable functions are not even parsed | blaze / relax | Implemented |
| One-file cache. Only entries used this time are written back, so GC is automatic | relax store | Implemented |
| Per-function sections, Local symbols, `-no-pie`, `--gc-sections`, strip | wild | Implemented |
| Cache the link line and start the linker (wild) directly | wild measurement | Implemented |
| Skip linking if the object is identical | - | Implemented |
| Thread parallelism only when there are many misses (cold). Each thread parses only its assigned items | relax compile_split | Implemented |
| α-normalized hash (renaming local variables does not invalidate) | blaze | Not implemented |
| ICF (hash of code + relocation targets) | blaze dedupe | Not implemented |
| Monomorphization keyed by layout | blaze polymorph | Not implemented (no generics yet) |
| Own inlining + slot forwarding (with -O) | relax | Not implemented |
| Embedding libwild, objects in memory | wild | Not implemented |
| Incremental linking (slack + jump table) | blaze patch-in-place | Not implemented |

# 調査メモ: blaze / relax / wild

日付: 2026-11-14

zustc の設計に使うため、3 つのプロジェクトを読んで整理した（2026-11-14 時点の main をソースで読んだだけで、ビルドはしていない。wild だけは crates.io の 0.10.0 を入れて実際に使った）。

- blaze: https://github.com/indexable-inc/blaze
- relax: https://github.com/makepad/relax
- wild: https://github.com/wild-linker/wild

## 一覧

| | blaze | relax | wild |
|---|---|---|---|
| 何か | cargo の代わり。常駐 daemon が rustc を使わずにビルドする | Rust の JIT とライブコンパイラ | 高速な ELF リンカ |
| フロントエンド | rust-analyzer の fork（rowan、hir-def/hir-ty）。trait solver は rustc から vendor | 全部自前（lexer、Pratt parser、rustc から移植した typeck と next-solver）。依存クレートなし | - |
| IR | HIR → MIR → (CLIF / LIR) | typeck::Body → RIR（非 SSA の vreg、CFG） | - |
| バックエンド | 今は MIR → CLIF。v2 では開発ビルドを copy-and-patch stencil、リリースを LLVM にする方針で、ネイティブコード生成に Cranelift は使わない | 自前（interp → O1 → O3、linear scan regalloc） | - |
| コンパイル単位 | 単相化した関数インスタンス 1 個 | 関数インスタンス 1 個（初回呼び出しで lazy に） | 入力セクション |
| キャッシュキー | BLAKE3 で、本体を α 正規化しスパンは入れない。callee は interface hash だけ | 128bit。compiler ID + インスタンス + 依存の interface 指紋 + 本体 | - |
| リンク | 自前リンカ（約 89k 行）。in-place patch とジャンプテーブル | リンカなし（JIT）。startup image あり | 並列。`--gc-sections` は既定で有効、ICF なし、LTO はプラグイン経由のみ |

## blaze から真似できること

1. **関数単位キャッシュ + callee は interface hash だけ**（`crates/blaze-codegen/src/template.rs`）。
   コンパイル済みコードは callee を「参照リストの位置」で持つので、callee の本体を編集しても caller は再コンパイルされない。リロケーションの名前が付け替わるだけ。
   → zustc でそのまま採用した（`Blob` のリロケーションは関数 ID か名前で持つ）。
2. **本体ハッシュに空白・コメント・スパンを入れない**（`docs/v2/plan/design/item-hash.md`）。
   blaze はさらにローカル変数を de Bruijn 風の index に α 正規化するので、ローカル変数のリネームでも無効化されない。
   → zustc は lexer レベルの正規化まで。α 正規化はまだ。
3. **到達可能性**：main、テスト、export から到達するものだけをコンパイルする。
4. **ICF とポリモーフ化はリンカではなくコンパイラでやる**：
   - レイアウト（size/align/ABI）でキーを作るので `Vec<A>` と `Vec<B>` が共有できる。
   - コード + リロケーション先のハッシュで同一関数を畳む（`dedupe.rs`）。
   - 定数だけが違う関数をパラメータ化する（`fold.rs`）。
5. **開発ビルドではシンボル名を短いハッシュにし、line table だけにする**。
6. **増分リンク**：`.text` に余白を残しておき、変更された関数は末尾に追記し、ジャンプテーブル経由で呼ぶ。リンクが支配的になってから検討すれば十分。
7. **やらなくていいもの**：daemon、DBSP、stencil。モノレポ規模の仕組みで、個人用には過剰。

## relax から真似できること

1. **demand-driven**：名前解決も型検査も、到達したものだけ行う（`front/src/lazy.rs`、`demand.rs`）。AOT なら「main からの到達集合だけをコンパイル」になる。
2. **キャッシュ形式**（`compiler/src/cache.rs`、`store.rs`）：
   - 1 クレート = 1 ファイル。ヘッダの後にソート済みの index、その後に append-only の payload。A/B の index スロットを切り替えて crash-safe にしている。
   - リロケーションは安定な ID（定義キー、文字列のバイト列など）で保存する。
   - インライン展開したときは、取り込んだ関数のキーも記録する。
   → zustc も 1 ファイルにした。index + payload で、デコードはヒットしたときだけ。
3. **自前の小さな std**（約 120k 行）。rust-src をコンパイルしないので、ビルド時間もバイナリも小さくなる。
4. **最適化 tier の要点**（LLVM 比 1.12x）：
   - インライン展開（rustc のコストモデル）。
   - スタックスロットの SROA 系。Cranelift には SROA がないので、ここは自前で書く必要がある。
   - LICM、値域解析による境界チェック削除。
5. **パーサはエラー回復なしで最初のエラーで止まる**。個人用ならそれで十分。

## wild から真似できること / zustc 側でやるべきこと

1. **オブジェクトの出し方**：
   - 関数ごとにセクションを分ける（`ObjectBuilder::per_function_section(true)`）。これがないと `--gc-sections` で何も消えない。
   - export しないものは Local/hidden にする。
   - `-no-pie` で `R_*_RELATIVE` を出さない。
   - 文字列は `SHF_MERGE|SHF_STRINGS` セクションに置く。ただし merge セクションは GC されないので、死んだデータを入れないこと。
2. **LTO は linker plugin（LLVM bitcode / GIMPLE）だけ**。Cranelift には該当する IR がないので、wild はただのネイティブリンカになる。
   **インライン展開、DCE、単相化の重複除去、ICF はコンパイラ側で whole-program にやるしかない。**
   → zustc は 1 プログラム = 1 オブジェクトにして、到達可能性による DCE をコンパイラ側でやっている。
3. **cc ドライバを経由しない**：
   - 実測で、cc + lld は 21ms、wild の直接起動は 5ms だった。
   - `libwild` クレートを使えばライブラリとして呼べるし、`FileSystem` trait でオブジェクトをメモリから直接渡せる。`.o` を書く必要がなくなる。
4. **増分リンクは wild の最終目標だが、まだ実装されていない**。
5. 実装テクニック：
   - mmap して `'data` で借用し、コピーしない。
   - `u32` の dense ID と Vec の表を使う。
   - 名前のハッシュは 1 回だけ計算して使い回す。
   - 出力を先にサイズ決めしてから、互いに素な `&mut` スライスに分けて並列に書く。
   - fork して後片付けを裏に回す。

## zustc で採用したもの（優先度順）

| アイデア | 出典 | 状態 |
|---|---|---|
| 関数単位の機械語キャッシュ。callee はシグネチャだけをキーに入れる | blaze template / relax cache | 実装済み |
| 空白・コメントを無視したアイテムハッシュ（自前 lexer） | blaze item-hash | 実装済み |
| 変更したアイテムだけ syn で parse（要約キャッシュ） | relax demand / blaze early cutoff | 実装済み |
| main からの到達可能性。到達しない関数は parse もしない | blaze / relax | 実装済み |
| 1 ファイルキャッシュ。今回使ったエントリだけ書き戻すので自動 GC になる | relax store | 実装済み |
| 関数ごとのセクション、Local シンボル、`-no-pie`、`--gc-sections`、strip | wild | 実装済み |
| リンク行をキャッシュして、リンカ（wild）を直接起動する | wild 実測 | 実装済み |
| オブジェクトが同一ならリンクを省略 | - | 実装済み |
| ミスの多いとき（cold）だけスレッド並列。各スレッドは担当アイテムだけを parse | relax compile_split | 実装済み |
| α 正規化ハッシュ（ローカル変数のリネームで無効化しない） | blaze | 未実装 |
| ICF（コード + リロケーション先のハッシュ） | blaze dedupe | 未実装 |
| レイアウトをキーにした単相化 | blaze polymorph | 未実装（ジェネリクスがまだない） |
| 自前インライン + slot forwarding（-O 時） | relax | 未実装 |
| libwild の埋め込み、メモリ上のオブジェクト | wild | 未実装 |
| 増分リンク（余白 + ジャンプテーブル） | blaze patch-in-place | 未実装 |

# Incremental builds of generated programs (N = 1000 / 5000)

Date: 2026-11-15

## N = 1000 functions (320KB)

The environment is a Linux x86-64 cloud container (about 4 cores). rustc 1.97.0, wild 0.10.0, Cranelift 0.137.
Measured with programs of "N functions + mutual calls" generated by `bench/gen.py`. The output of every tool matched the result of running the rustc build.

| tool | cold ms | no-op ms | 1-function edit ms | peak RSS (cold) | binary | cache / incr dir |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| zustc (starting wild directly) | 128 | 11.7 | **19.0** | **13.4 MiB** | 413 KiB | **498 KiB** |
| zustc (starting bfd directly) | 129 | 12.1 | 33.2 | 13.2 MiB | 422 KiB | 498 KiB |
| zustc (starting lld directly) | 141 | 12.0 | 36.7 | 58.7 MiB | 412 KiB | 498 KiB |
| rustc `-Cincremental -Cdebuginfo=0` | 887 | 217 | 461 | 164 MiB | 5013 KiB | 22151 KiB |
| rustc `-Cincremental -Cdebuginfo=2` | 1015 | 218 | 563 | 183 MiB | 5557 KiB | 24592 KiB |
| rustc `-O` (reference, non-incremental) | 12445 | - | - | 147 MiB | 382 KiB | - |

## N = 5000 functions (1.6MB)

| tool | cold ms | no-op ms | 1-function edit ms | peak RSS (cold) | binary | cache / incr dir |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| zustc (starting wild directly) | 497 | 63.6 | **87.0** | **34.4 MiB** | 2030 KiB | **2479 KiB** |
| zustc (starting bfd directly) | 471 | 53.9 | 87.0 | 34.6 MiB | 2038 KiB | 2479 KiB |
| rustc `-Cincremental -Cdebuginfo=0` | 3810 | 756 | 1911 | 499 MiB | 8040 KiB | 113644 KiB |

Compared with rustc, a 1-function edit is 20–24 times faster, cold RSS is 1/12–1/14, and the cache is 1/45.
The no-op at 5000 functions takes around 60ms because lexing the whole file, rebuilding the `.o`, and reading and writing the cache are proportional to N.
With multiple files and per-file item summaries, this could also become O(amount of change).

Breakdown of zustc for a 1-function edit (`--time`, N=1000):

| Phase | ms |
|---|---:|
| lex | 2.6 |
| item summary (parse only 1 item) | 1.3 |
| plan | 0.9 |
| cache lookup | 0.5 |
| codegen (1 function) | 0.4 |
| .o generation | 3.6 |
| cache save | 1.2 |
| link (wild) | 5.6 |
| **Total** | **15.9 (peak RSS 12 MiB)** |

The output size of hello (`examples/hello.rs`) is 6.0 KiB with zustc and 333 KiB with rustc debug (stripped).
Most of the rustc output comes from std.

# Comparison with rustc (as of 2026-11-15, after adding overflow checks, panic messages, etc.)

Date: 2026-11-15

The environment has no wild installed, so the linker is chosen automatically (ld.lld).

Build time (`python3 bench/run.py 1000`, N = 1000 functions):

| tool | cold ms | no-op ms | 1-function edit ms | peak RSS (cold) | binary | cache / incr dir |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| zustc | 167 | 20 | **44** | **59 MiB** | 553 KiB | **642 KiB** |
| rustc `-Cincremental -Cdebuginfo=0` | 962 | 230 | 433 | 163 MiB | 5013 KiB | 22151 KiB |
| rustc `-O` (non-incremental) | 11604 | - | - | 147 MiB | 382 KiB | - |

A 1-function edit is about 10 times faster than rustc incremental. zustc is slower than in the earlier table (wild, before adding checks) because of the linker difference (wild 5ms / ld.lld 17ms), and because of the checks and the panic table.

Speed of the generated code (`python3 bench/runtime.py`, `bench/rt/*.rs`. Builds without cache; median of 3 runs for both build and execution. All outputs match rustc):

| Program | zustc | zustc `-O` | rustc (debug) | rustc `-O` | build ms (zustc / rustc debug / rustc -O) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| fib (recursive fib(35)) | 86 ms (3.1x) | 68 ms (2.5x) | 97 ms (3.5x) | 27 ms | 44 / 106 / 127 |
| hashmap (1 million entry calls) | 212 ms (1.9x) | 144 ms (1.3x) | 723 ms (6.5x) | 112 ms | 55 / 162 / 289 |
| matmul (200×200, 5 times) | 225 ms (5.2x) | 94 ms (2.2x) | 657 ms (15x) | 43 ms | 67 / 168 / 268 |

reference.quote:
# Disk usage of incremental builds

Date: 2026-11-15

- The cache (`.crcache`) does not hold per-function machine code. The machine code is in the output `.o`, so the cache only stores (length, hash),
  and the next build walks the symtab of the previous `.o` to take out the same machine code (if the hash does not match, or there is no `.o`, it recompiles).
  Only functions that are called from nowhere and were not placed in the `.o` are written to the cache together with their machine code.
- The `.text` of the `.o` that is kept is an ELF standard compressed section (`SHF_COMPRESSED`, zstd level 1) (`src/elfz.rs`).
  - wild decompresses `SHF_COMPRESSED` in any input section when reading, so the compressed `.o` is passed as-is.
  - ld.lld 18 crashes on compressed `SHF_ALLOC` sections, and ld.bfd fails with "reloc against ...: error 4" (in the gABI, compression is for non-ALLOC sections).
    For these two, an uncompressed `.o` is passed as a temporary file (`<out>.tmp.o`, deleted after linking).
- The `.o` combines everything into one `.text`. Which functions to place is decided by following relocations and vtables from main / exports (instead of `--gc-sections`).

Changes on gen1000 (310 KB of source):

| | Initial | After removing machine code from the cache | After compressing `.text` | After packing the index and the panic table |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `.crcache` | 642 KiB | 116 KiB | 116 KiB | **38 KiB** |
| `.o` | 757 KiB | 631 KiB | 153 KiB | **67 KiB** |
| Total | 1399 KiB | 747 KiB | 270 KiB | **105 KiB** (the rustc incremental directory is 22156 KiB) |
| Binary | 553 KiB | 553 KiB | 553 KiB | 519 KiB |

- The cache file compresses its body with zstd, and writes keys as the low 64 bits and lengths as variable-length integers (an index entry goes from 20 bytes to about 9 bytes. Compression also shrinks the item summaries and panic locations to 1/3).
- The panic table became a byte sequence of variable-length integers, and it refers only to the start of `.text` (function positions are counted by the builder itself when making the `.o`, and checked against the symtab).
  Before, it was 24 bytes of relocation + 16 bytes of header per function, and 8 bytes per location. The table is also in the binary, so the binary also became 6% smaller.
  The handler (`__exr_on_trap`) reads the sequence from the front on panic.
- The `.o` compresses not only `.text` but also the PROGBITS loaded into memory (the panic table, strings) (wild decompresses all of them when reading).

`python3 bench/run.py 1000` (with wild 0.10.0 on PATH):

| tool | cold ms | no-op ms | 1-function edit ms | peak RSS (cold) | binary | cache + .o |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| zustc (wild) | 124 | 17 | **28** | 19.5 MiB | 554 KiB | **270 KiB** |
| zustc (ld.lld, uncompressed temporary `.o`) | 151 | 18 | 41 | 59.0 MiB | 553 KiB | 270 KiB |

- Compression goes from 587 KB → 69 KB in 0.3 ms (`compress` in `--time`). Linking with wild, including decompression, takes 6–9 ms.

# Making strings and sort faster with `-O`

Date: 2026-11-15

| | Before | After | rustc -O |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| strings `-O` | 141 ms | **73 ms** | 34 ms |
| sort `-O` | 550 ms | **195 ms** | 190 ms |
| strings (debug) | 259 ms | 113 ms | (rustc debug 121 ms) |
| sort (debug) | 725 ms | 252 ms | (rustc debug 1983 ms) |

- Formatting (callgrind showed integer formatting at 41%):
  - For integers in `{}` (decimal, no width or sign specifier), fill the digits from the back and append them all at once (no more temporary String and per-character push; division by 10 becomes a multiplication)
  - The String of `format!` reserves the length of the fixed parts + 8 bytes per argument up front
  - `Vec::truncate` only changes the length if the elements need no drop (added `core::mem::needs_drop`). `extend_from_slice` is a memcpy
  - Arrays filled with an integer constant (`[0u8; 24]`) are written 8 bytes at a time, and copies of aggregates with small alignment are also 8 bytes at a time (before, 1 byte at a time)
  - `split`'s next copies the fields into locals before looping
- sort:
  - `sort` on integers of 64 bits or less, and `sort_by_key` with an integer key, use a stable LSD radix sort (digits whose byte is the same in all elements are skipped).
    sort_by_key calls the key function only once per element (std calls it per comparison, so the number of calls differs from std).
    (I also tried computing the keys once and then sorting indices or (key, index) pairs, but the random reads and writes of the permutation made it slower)
  - Per-type branches in the prelude (`if __exr_int_kind::<T>() == 0` / `needs_drop::<T>()`) are decided by the type, so the unused side is not compiled (and no instances are created)
- Size: programs that sort integers get the radix sort added (sorting's binary +42%, ordering's cache +49%). Programs that use formatting also grow a little. The budgets were re-recorded.
- What remains in the cache: the panic location table (4–5 bytes per location), relocations, item summaries (21 KB), the entry index (20 bytes per entry, about 40 KB). Integers are variable-length, and offsets and lines are written as differences from the previous value.

zustc binaries have no symbols (stripping gives the same size). rustc links std statically, so even after strip it is 335 KiB or more. zustc compiles only the parts of the prelude that are used and links libc dynamically, so its binaries are 1/10–1/30 of rustc's.

- 書式化（callgrind で整数の書式化が 41%）：
  - `{}` の整数（10 進・幅と符号の指定なし）は、桁を後ろから詰めてまとめて足す（一時の String と 1 文字ずつの push をやめた。10 の割り算は掛け算になる）

  - `Vec::truncate` は drop の要らない要素なら長さを変えるだけ（`core::mem::needs_drop` を足した）。`extend_from_slice` は memcpy
  - 整数の定数で埋める配列（`[0u8; 24]`）は 8 byte ずつ書き、アラインメントの小さい集約型の写しも 8 byte ずつ（前は 1 byte ずつ）
  - `split` の next はフィールドをローカルに写してから回す
- sort：
  - 64 bit 以下の整数の `sort` と、キーが整数の `sort_by_key` は、安定な LSD 基数ソート（全要素で同じバイトの桁は飛ばす）。
    sort_by_key のキーの関数は要素ごとに 1 回だけ呼ぶ（std は比較ごとに呼ぶので、呼ばれる回数は std と違う）。
    （キーを 1 回だけ計算してから添字や (キー, 添字) を並べる方法も試したが、並べ替えのランダムな読み書きで遅くなった）

# matmul and sieve with `-O`, generics and monomorphization

Date: 2026-11-15

| | Before | After | rustc -O |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| matmul `-O` | 77 ms | **53 ms** | 31 ms |
| sieve `-O` | 252 ms | **144 ms** | 92 ms |
| nbody `-O` | 92 ms | **69 ms** | 42 ms |

- Hoisting out of loops (`-O`): the start and length of indexed receivers that do not change in the body (and condition) of a for / while are read before the loop.
  - Targets are local Vecs, `&Vec` / `&mut Vec` arguments (`c` / `b`), and rows indexed by variables that do not change in the loop (`c[i]` / `b[k]`).
    The receiver must appear in the body only in the form `x[..]..` (a read, or an assignment to a scalar element), with no method receiver, `&mut`, re-binding, macro or closure.
  - The row is read before the loop; if out of range, the read location becomes a dummy area (`select`). The check `i < c.len()` is done inside the body, using the value compared beforehand (the order of panics does not change).
  - The inner loop of matmul went from 30 instructions → 12 instructions (the re-reads of `c` and `c[i]` disappeared).
- `vec![x; n]` no longer calls push and writes directly into the allocated area (memset for 1-byte elements). The 20 million pushes in sieve's initialization disappeared.
- `for (i, x) in v.iter().enumerate()` binds i and x without building a tuple (the stores to the stack and the reloads disappeared; sieve's instruction count went from 615M → 535M).
- Instances that produce the same machine code are placed only once (ICF: `Vec<u32>::push` and `Vec<i32>::push`, etc.). Instances whose machine code, relocations (callees rewritten to the representative), data, vtables, panic locations and calling convention are the same are folded, repeating until nothing changes.
  The cache looks up machine code in the `.o` by (length, hash), so folded instances also hit with the representative's machine code. Across all examples, binaries −3% (binary_heap −13%), `.o` −3%.
- `__exr_drop_in_place::<T>` / `drop(x)` are not called for types that need no drop (and no instances are created; collections went from 353 → 341 instances).

# Things learned along the way

Date: 2026-11-15

- **On cold builds, all the syn ASTs for item summaries were kept, so RSS reached 162MB at 5000 functions**.
  Making the item summary parsing parallel and discarding the ASTs inside the threads brought RSS to 35MB, and cold from 855ms to 526ms.
- **The first version parsed the whole file with syn**. So even a no-op took 114ms, and on cold builds each parallel thread re-parsed the whole file, bringing RSS to 191 MiB.
  Switching to the own lexer and the item summary cache brought no-op to 12ms and cold RSS to 39 MiB.
- **Linking was dominated by the number of process stages in the cc driver**. cc + lld takes 21ms, starting ld.lld directly 17ms, starting wild directly 5ms.
- Cranelift's `single_pass` regalloc compiles fast, but execution is about 40% slower (table above).

# What regression monitoring caught

Date: 2026-11-15

Examples where the regression monitoring (`bench/regress.sh`) of size budgets, criterion and `tests/compare.sh` actually did its job. All of them were fixed without loosening budgets or thresholds.

- Size
  - Adding enums made item summaries grow by 1 byte/item. Fixed by packing the item summary encoding.
  - The "checked" mark grew by 4 bytes/function. It is now not written when empty.
  - The whole prelude was being attached, so every cache grew by about 2.3 KB. Now only what is used is attached.
  - The field names `min` / `max` pulled in the functions of `core::cmp`. Now only when the identifier `core` appears.
- Speed
  - no_std support made LSP 1-function edits +31% slower and no-op builds +10% slower.
  - To remove noise depending on the time of day, the baseline commit was benchmarked at the same time in a worktree, and the cause was narrowed down with callgrind.
  - What was fixed: hashing all identifiers every time (prelude selection), the LSP hashing the whole file contents, and SipHash in the name table.
  - The name table was switched to our own FxHasher. It is not used for cache keys.
  - As a result, LSP 1-function edits became −7% and no-op builds −4%, faster than the baseline.
- Correctness (when adding closures and dyn; found by adding a stage to `tests/compare.sh` that compares both "no cache" and "rebuild from cache")
  - Closures in the same function all get the same struct deep hash (= the parent item's hash) and signature. So the cache keys of `consume::<closure#8>` and `consume::<closure#9>` collided, and the second build used another closure's machine code. Fixed by putting the closure's name in the key.
  - vtables were defined as zero-init, so they were placed in `.bss`, relocations were not applied, and null was called.
- Speed (when adding closures and dyn)
  - An A/B against HEAD showed +4% on LSP 1-function edits. The causes were a `Vec` clone per type inference call and including names in struct hashes; both were removed.
  - By callgrind instruction counts, 1-function edits (`Session::check`) became fewer than HEAD. didOpen (cold) was about +2%, with no significant difference in criterion either.
- When adding function pointers and Box
  - `Ty` had grown from 16 → 24 bytes (because the earlier `Dyn(&'static str)` was a fat pointer). Changed to `&'static String` to get back to 16 bytes.
  - criterion showed LSP 1-function edits +14% and lexer +10%. But the lexer code had not changed.
  - callgrind showed that `b"..".contains(&c)` in `lexer::St::tok` had become a memchr. The call count was the same; only the instruction count grew by +32% (a difference in the placement of static strings).
  - Switching to `matches!` gave, versus the baseline, LSP 1-function edits −5%, no-op builds −13%, lexer −6%.
- When adding Drop (added a valgrind stage to `tests/compare.sh`: it fails on memory errors and definite leaks)
  - Reading `*b` was treated as a move of `b`, and the Box leaked. The contents of a deref are now read without moving.
  - `self.top = n.next` (moving only a field of the Box contents) treated the whole `n` as moved, so nodes leaked.
    The moved field is now filled with 0 (a null Box / `None`), and the owner is dropped normally.
  - Two existing bugs were also found.
    - Returning `&Rect { .. }` as `&'static` pointed to a temporary on the stack. Constant expressions are now promoted to static data, as in rustc.
    - The type of the tuple struct field `n.0` was not inferred.
  - Programs that use neither Box nor Drop generate no drop handling at all (`Program::has_drop`). Speed and size budgets do not change.
- When adding Vec / String
  - criterion showed +20–40% on almost every item, but the unchanged lexer was just as slow; it was noise from machine load.
    Measured side by side with HEAD in the same time slot, it was within about ±10% noise. callgrind instruction counts were also at or below HEAD.
  - The only real increase was prelude selection (+26%). The cause was more prelude names, which made the candidate tables per first byte longer. Switched to a table looked up by (first byte, length), bringing it below HEAD.
  - `==` does not appear as an identifier, so the prelude's `Vec::eq` / `String::eq` were not attached, and pointers were compared. eq is now attached together with the type, and also added to the reachability roots.
- When adding Iterator
  - Size budgets were exceeded in almost every example (hello's cache went from 3.2 KB → 10.8 KB). `for x in v.iter()`, the variable name `count`, `a.max(b)`, `Option::take` and the field `.next` pulled in all the iterator parts.
    The conditions for attaching were narrowed, e.g. to "a call that creates an iterator followed by an adapter or consuming method", so the existing examples pass without loosening their budgets by even 1 byte.
  - On LSP 1-function edits, prelude selection was +63% (because there were more candidate names). The result is now remembered in the Session per item hash, and unchanged items are not scanned. In callgrind, `Session::check` is below HEAD.
  - Type inference recorded the types of macro arguments it parsed temporarily by address, so nodes created by codegen landed on freed addresses and looked up the type of another expression (`&str`). Temporary nodes are no longer recorded.
  - Editing one closure rebuilt 65 instances of the map etc. that receive it. Removing the parent item's hash from the closure struct's deep hash brought this to 18 (just the parent and the closures).
- When adding format! / HashMap
  - nostd_core's cache went from 8.7 KB → 22.7 KB. `write` in a raw pointer's `p.write(v)` and `a.max(b)` pulled in all the formatting parts and String / Vec.
    Formatting macro names are now counted only in the form `name!`, and `__exr_str_cmp` is no longer attached for max / min.
  - iterators got HashMap's iterators (`HmIter` etc., on the `impl Iterator for` side). These are also attached only when the HashMap name is present.
  - The formatting helpers (`__exr_fmt_int` etc.) were made generic `<G>` and removed from the roots. Only the ones called are compiled, as instances.
    Non-generic functions called from instance bodies (`__exr_print` → `putchar`) are picked up by expanding the live set after each codegen wave.
  - The only budget loosened was vec_string's cache (45.0 KB → 48.5 KB). For `name.to_string()`, the receiver type is not known at selection time (integers need Display), so the formatting parts get attached.
  - callgrind: gen1000 build +0.15%, check −4%. Examples that use a lot of the prelude grew (iterators +5%, vec_string +15%, due to more prelude being attached).
- When adding ordering comparisons (PartialOrd / Ord)
  - Always attaching the comparison glue (`__exr_cmp`) made the caches of small examples grow by 20 bytes each and exceed the budgets.
    Recursive types go through Box / Vec, so the glue is attached only to programs that use those, and elsewhere codegen expands comparisons in place.
  - `cmp` in `use core::cmp::{max, min}` and the bound `T: Ord` attached the trait declaration and `Ordering`. `cmp::` is no longer counted as a path, and the trait declaration is attached only when there is a hand-written `impl Ord for`. No existing budget was loosened by even 1 byte.
  - Existing bugs found along the way
    - Temporaries of `println!` in a block's tail expression or in a match arm were dropped at the end of the statement, which failed Cranelift's verifier (value dominance) (`if c { println!(..) } else { .. }`).
      Temporaries in tail expressions and match arms are now dropped on the spot (the same as Rust 2024).
    - `len()` on `&&&str` followed only one level and returned 0.
    - `None` / `Ordering::Less` on the right side of a comparison were read as places (local variables).
  - callgrind: gen1000 build −2.6%, check −6.8%, examples that use the prelude +0.4–1.5%.
- When adding merge sort, binary_search and clamp (`examples/sorting.rs`)
  - sort is insertion sort in groups of 16 + bottom-up merging (the work area is n elements via realloc). Elements are moved bitwise with `read` / `write`, so there is no double free even for types with Drop (checked with valgrind).
    sort of a 200,000-element `Vec<u64>` went from 56 seconds → 0.04 seconds.
  - Size budgets were raised for examples that use sort (vec_string +3%, ordering +16%, etc.). The merge sort body is larger than insertion sort, and there is an instance per element type and comparison closure.
    vec_string's build is also +9% (callgrind; due to more functions to compile). Programs that do not use sort do not change (gen1000 ±0%).
  - Existing bugs found along the way
    - Integer methods with a `&mut u64` / `&u64` receiver (`s.wrapping_mul(..)`) computed on the address instead of the pointee.
    - Variants with paths of 3 or more segments, like `std::cmp::Ordering::Less`, were looked up by the second segment's name (`cmp`).
    - `==` / `!=` on raw pointers did not work.
- When adding BinaryHeap and sort_by_cached_key
  - No existing size budget item changed (BinaryHeap is attached only when its name is present).
  - callgrind: since the prelude got larger, the once-per-process lexing of the prelude is +0.5M instructions (+3.8% on hello, about 0.1 ms). gen1000 build ±0%.
    The check measurement has about ±8% noise at 1000 functions (even HEAD vs HEAD gives 1.82G–1.92G), so it was measured 3 times each to confirm there was no difference.
- When adding BinaryHeap append / extend
  - Type inference unified `Item = T` of `Vec<T>::extend` with the `&i32` of `v.extend(w.iter())`, making `v` a `Vec<&i32>`. extend now decides v's element type from the argument's element type (the pointee for references, except `&str`).
  - Existing bug found along the way: the type of `to_string()` on `&&str` could not be inferred, so the return value of the closure in `a.iter().map(|s| s.to_string())` was not determined.
  - Size budgets and callgrind (gen1000 / hello / vec_string / binary_heap) were all within ±1%.
- When adding commonly used features in bulk (`tests/probe.sh`: compares small programs in `tests/probe/*.rs` against rustc and counts how many pass; it started at 2 / 28)
  - The prelude reached nearly 4000 lines, and the once-per-process lexing of the prelude took half of hello's build (8M instructions).
    The splitting was moved to build.rs (using `src/lexer.rs` as-is), and the prelude body was put in `src/prelude_lib.rs.in`. hello went from 14.9M → 9.3M instructions.
  - The string helpers and operator traits made the size budgets of existing examples exceed across the board (nostd_core's cache 8.7 KB → 29.7 KB, etc.).
    - Helpers with the same names as integer `to_ascii_uppercase` or `Option::replace` are attached only when there is a String or string literal receiver
    - Operator trait declarations only when there is a hand-written `impl Add for ..`
    - New String methods were made generic `<G>` (they were considered live by method name alone, so Vec's `pop` etc. caused String's `pop` to be compiled too)
    - Helpers that looped over chars now read UTF-8 directly and do not attach the iterator parts
    No existing budget was loosened by even 1 byte.
- When adding floating point, i128, standard I/O, Rc/RefCell, `impl Iterator` return values, etc. (probe increased to 73 programs, all matching rustc)
  - Decimal conversion with glibc's `ecvt_r` sometimes got digits wrong, so it is done exactly with base-1e9 multi-precision arithmetic. The random cross-checks of `examples/float_fuzz.rs` (6000 lines) and `examples/int128.rs` match rustc.
  - For size budgets, new prelude types are "attached only when their name appears" (owner gating), so most items did not need to change. The limits were raised only for iterators (+68 B), text_more (+0.4%) and hashmap (+0.3%, for `cycle`, a default method of Iterator).
  - callgrind (instruction counts): hello went from 9.96M before the work → 9.95M (dropping a `Vec` allocation when building the prelude item table offset the increase). gen1000 is 2.43G, with no difference within the ±2% noise seen even between HEAD builds.
- When adding overflow checks
  - callgrind: gen1000 build 2.43G → 2.55G instructions (+5%); `-O` is 3.06G, the same as HEAD. hello 9.95M → 10.25M (for registering the handler in main).
    At first, each check created its own panic branch and block, giving +50% (3.67G). Switched to `trapnz`, and skipped checks for constant divisors and shift amounts.
  - Size: code grows by the amount of the checks (gen1000's binary 443 KB → 498 KB; no growth with `-O`). This is the same kind of growth as rustc debug builds, so the budgets were re-recorded with UPDATE_BUDGET=1.
  - Existing bugs found along the way: double free when returning a String error with `?`, `{ return None; }` having type `()`, enum `==` following pointers of unused variants, `saturating_add` using a vector instruction, `struct Node { children: Vec<Node> }` being "infinitely sized", instantiation never stopping when `Node<T>` holds `Option<Box<Node<T>>>`, char literal patterns, the addresses of expressions rebuilt inside type inference overlapping codegen nodes, and so on.
  - When trying to decide the return value of `|a| a + 1` from the callee's bound (`B`), the not-yet-determined `B` was given priority over the parent's type inference (`map(|w| w.parse().unwrap())`).
- When emitting panic messages per kind
  - The runtime handler (table lookup, number printing, messages) is always attached to std programs, so small examples grew by +3–6 KB (hello's binary 6.0 KB → 10.0 KB).
    At first it was +6–7 KB. Fixed: the formatted panic function pulled in String / Vec (it is now attached only to programs that use formatting),
    the sigaction struct was built by array initialization (made static), and messages were selected with an if chain (changed to a concatenated string and a position table).
  - The table was at first 16 bytes per location, making gen1000's object +15%. Packing a 20-bit offset, 13-bit message number, and 31 bits of kind, line and column into one word made it +8% (the cache, in the same form, +5%). The budgets were re-recorded with UPDATE_BUDGET=1.
  - callgrind: gen1000 build 2.54G → 2.57G (+1%), `-O` 3.06G → 3.11G. hello's no-cache build 10.3M → 29M (parsing and codegen of the handler functions; about 4 ms), rebuild with cache 2.8M → 5.6M.
  - Existing bug found along the way: `__FmtError` did not implement Debug (unwrap of `Result<_, fmt::Error>`).
- When resolving `==` between different types via the PartialEq trait
  - Naming: methods of `impl PartialEq<R> for S` whose right-hand type differs from the self type are named `S::<PartialEq<R>>::eq` (the same as `S::<Display>::fmt` for Display / Debug). `==` looks for that candidate only when lt and rt differ, so same-type comparisons work as before.
  - Type inference: when both sides of `==` are a Vec and an array or slice, the elements are unified only when they are numeric literals (`v == [1, 2]` with v: Vec<i64>). `Vec<String> == Vec<&str>` is not unified.
  - Size: programs that compare arrays get the impl attached, and caches are +0.1–1.7% (enums +256 B, etc.). callgrind: gen1000 and hello ±0%, vec_string +2% (parsing of the attached prelude).
- When printing the left / right values of assert_eq!
  - Programs that did not use formatting get the formatting parts attached (options' binary 16.7 KB → 23.9 KB, build 57M → 125M instructions). This is what is needed to print the values with `{:?}`, so the budgets were re-recorded. gen1000 and hello ±0%.
  - Existing bugs found along the way:
    - The line of a panic location was the line within the item (lines of the second and later functions were off). dbg! had the same problem.
    - Programs that use no prelude names at all (traits etc.) did not get the panic handler, so a panic was SIGILL (exit code 132).
    - `&None` was treated as a borrow of a variable.
- When adding iterators, Vec and clone
  - **Until now, `.clone()` on `#[derive(Clone)]` types did not work, and clone of `Vec<String>` and `cloned()` were bitwise copies (double free)**. Fixed by adding clone glue.
  - The `impl Iterator` of the new adapters (Rev / Peekable / FlatMap etc.) were all attached to any program that used iterators. Now only when that struct is needed.
    The Formatter's `fill` field in formatting pulled in `Vec::fill` and the whole clone set, so the field was renamed. No existing budget was loosened.
  - The temporary Vec in `vec![..].join(..)` was not dropped (found with valgrind).
  - callgrind: gen1000 ±0%, hello +2.5%, vec_string / iterators / hashmap +0.5–1%.
- When adding closures inside macro arguments
  - The item summary and codegen parse only macro arguments that contain `|` to count closures. callgrind: gen1000 +0.2%, iterators +0.7%, formatting ±0%.
  - Type inference keeps the re-parsed nodes of `vec![..]` arguments until the end of inference, so closure bodies can be deferred until the callee's bound is known (`vec![v.iter().map(|x| x * x).sum::<i32>(); 2]`).

# Multiple files and multiple crates (`zustc build <workspace>`)

Date: 2026-11-16

- `mod x;` reads `x.rs` / `x/mod.rs` (`src/srcmap.rs`). To keep line numbers unchanged, `mod x;` is blanked out and its contents are appended at the end of the file
  as `pub mod x { .. }`, with a table from lines of the combined source → (file, line). Errors become `file:line:col:`
- The workspace file has one crate per line (`lib <name> <root> [deps..]` / `bin <name> <root> [deps..]`). A .o is built per crate and they are linked at the end
- Crate C is analyzed as "C's source + the sources of the crates it depends on, appended as `pub mod name { .. }`".
  Non-generic functions and statics of dependency crates are in that crate's .o, so they are not compiled and are called by symbol. Instances of generic functions and
  the prelude are placed locally in each .o. Names inside a crate's modules are always `name__Item` (the same symbol no matter which crate it is analyzed with).
  `crate::` inside a crate means that crate, and `pub use` re-exports are followed too
- The panic table is placed per crate, and the executable's table points to the list of dependency crates' tables (`_xT_<name>`). The table holds the file mapping and
  a table of places where renaming shifted columns (`geom::f` → `geom__f` has the same length, but `f` → `geom__f` is longer), so panic locations are
  reported with the original file, line and column (`geom/src/lib.rs:13:37`, the same as rustc). The unwrap caller location (`__EXR_CALLER`) of the executable is shared by all
- Fingerprints: per crate, a hash of "compiler, settings, own source, interfaces of dependency crates" is written to `<name>.fp`, and if it is unchanged
  nothing is done. The interface hash includes only the signature for non-generic functions; for everything else (generic functions, traits, generic impls, `const fn`,
  `-> impl Trait`) it also includes the body and lines. So changing the body of a function in a depended-on crate does not recompile its users (only relinks)
- Out-of-date crates only use each other's sources (they do not wait for .o files), so they are compiled concurrently with fork. The cache is per crate (`<name>.crcache2`)
- `tests/workspace.rs`: compares tests/workspace (3 crates, 5 files: trait objects, statics, re-exports, Display) with rustc (rlib + link)
  (output, exit code, panic locations for division by zero / indexing / unwrap across crates and files). It also checks that a change to a function body rebuilds only that crate,
  and a change to a signature rebuilds its users too

`python3 bench/ws_bench.py --rustc` (6 lib × 8 files × 40 functions = 1920 functions + bin, 4 cores. rustc uses `-C incremental` rlib + link):

| Scenario | zustc build | rustc |
|---|---:|---:|
| cold | 489 ms | 3786 ms |
| no changes | 7 ms | 1043 ms |

# Speeding up the first half (front) of the self-hosted compiler

Date: 2026-11-16

Time spent in the first half when the zustc-built compiler (`tests/selfhost/build_compiler.py`) compiles itself (about 33 thousand lines)
(per-stage times from `ZUSTC_PROF=1 ... --time`. We counted where gdb stopped and fixed the most frequent places first):

| Stage | Initial | After | rustc-built compiler (after) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| macros | 9870 ms | 499 ms | 96 ms |
| flatten (flatten modules) | 2501 | 552 | 51 |
| hoist + ctor | 613 | 467 | 61 |
| split | 578 | 287 | 18 |
| prelude selection | 1219 | 74 | 16 |
| item summary | about 2400 | 1054 | 110 |
| program + refs | 862 | 645 | 72 |
| **front total** | **18159** | **3745** | **439** |

- macros: the lexer of our own proc_macro2 (mini_pm2) counted columns from the start of the line for every token (it now counts on from the previous one).
  `find_calls` / definition collection copied the contents of every bracket (brackets that contain no macro name are no longer walked).
  If the expansion contains no macro name, there is no further round. In addition, the whole source is scanned with the fast `lexer::tokenize`, and proc_macro2 only reads
  the inside of definitions and call brackets (`tests/macros_expand.rs` checks that the result is the same as the previous version, `expand_reference`)
- flatten: `iter_mut().take(n).skip(m)` used to fill a table walked from the start every time (replaced with an index loop)
- prelude selection: calls `contains` on the whole source about 40 times. The prelude's `str::find` now uses libc's `memmem`
  (this speeds up every program built with zustc)
- split: the item hash (the cache key) used two SipHashes. It now uses a mix of two multiply-and-rotate lanes (`src/key.rs`).
  It does not depend on how calls are split (it buffers 8 bytes at a time), so it gives the same value even when the Hash implementations in std and zustc's prelude split their write calls differently
- item summary: items are independent, so the work is split with fork (the same as function compilation in driver2). The parser's `punct_at` (called
  many times per operator precedence level) compares bytes, and does not search for operators at positions that are not symbols. The lexer looks at ASCII as raw bytes
- refs: before looking up the 4 tables, look up once in the set of names present in any of the tables
- The rest is the quality of the generated code (no inlining of small functions; `Iterator` adapters become function calls). The second half, codegen, takes 15.8 seconds
  (0.95 seconds for the rustc version), for the same reason

# Inlining small functions (driver2 `-O`)

Date: 2026-11-16

- minclif has no IR and turns instructions into machine code immediately, so inlining is done at the syntax tree level (`src/acg/p9_inline.rs`).
  Once the call's arguments have been built in ABI form (the copied address for aggregates passed by value, the destination for sret), instead of calling,
  the callee's body is code-generated into the same function. The body's parameters are bound to those values, and `return` / `?` / the tail value become
  a jump to the continuation block (checked by `emit_return`). The callee's type inference, scope and drop state are swapped in and restored afterwards
- Functions that are inlined: those whose body syntax tree is small (up to 1600 characters as a Debug string), that contain no closures, macros or nested items,
  and that are not special bodies (drop glue, etc.) or unwrap / expect that report the caller location. Both prelude and user functions (`Vec::len` /
  `Option::is_some` / `Parser::tok`, etc., about 300). Inside an inlined body, at most one more level; at most 400 times per function
- A caller that may inline user functions puts the callee item's hash and lines into its cache key. Panic locations are
  based on the callee's lines (the same location as rustc -O). Functions from dependency crates are not inlined (their bodies are not part of the interface
  hash, so if they change, the users would not be rebuilt)
- The callee's type inference does not depend on the caller, so it runs only once per instance (reused within the process)
- Functions called only from inlined bodies are not reachable from the caller's names: non-generic functions that the relocations of compiled machine code point to
  are also compiled (without this, they were undefined at link time)
- Along with this, minclif got a peephole optimization that skips instructions re-reading a value that was just written (`rax_holds`: if the previous instruction is
  "write rax to v's slot", do not read v. Cleared at the start of a block)
- `tests/driver2_inline.rs`: builds probe / examples / acg with and without `-O`, and checks that output, stderr and exit code are the same
- Effect (time for the self-hosted compiler to compile itself; each compared doing the same work with `ZUSTC_NO_INLINE=1`):
  no inlining 20.85 seconds → inlining 19.76 seconds → plus skipping re-reads 18.32 seconds (12% faster). Inlining makes the generated code 27% larger, and
  `-O` compilation about 20% slower (after reusing type inference). minclif places every value on the stack, so even when calls are
  removed, value loads and stores remain and the effect is small. Large speedups need register allocation

reference.quote:
# Register allocation in minclif

Date: 2026-11-16

minclif turned instructions into machine code immediately and placed every value in a stack slot (each instruction loads into rax / rcx and writes the result back).
Allocation needs to see the whole function, so it now assembles twice (`src/minclif.rs`):

1. **Recording and analysis**: `FunctionBuilder` records each called instruction as an `Op` (104 kinds, generated mechanically from Emitter's public methods) while
   assembling a first pass with the existing assembler (`Emitter`) (it decides value numbers and types, and returns the values and blocks that acg queries).
   The first pass records value and variable reads and writes (instruction numbers), segments (ranges where a block was written contiguously) and jump targets, and instructions that call functions
2. **Allocation** (`plan`): for a value written and read inside one segment, the live interval is that range; for values that cross segments (variables, block parameters, values live in loops),
   the range is extended to the end of the live segments using backward dataflow (whether it is live at segment entry and exit). Linear scan then
   assigns them to rbx, r12 to r15 (callee-saved: for intervals that cross calls) and rsi, rdi, r8 to r10 (for intervals with no calls).
   If registers run out, those with a small "number of reads and writes / length" go to slots. Floating point, i128, and values that use a slot directly (used
   as an address, or read and written with different widths) stay in slots. A call immediately followed by a trap (panic) does not return, so it does not count as crossing
3. **Final pass**: the Emitter, now holding the allocation, assembles the recorded instructions again. The existing instruction assembly is reused as-is,
   and value loads and stores (load_rax / store_rax, etc.) consult the allocation. Common instructions are written in register form: 64 / 32 bit
   add / sub / and / or / xor / imul and cmp become `mov d, a; op d, b`, constants are used directly, and load / store use `[base + off]`.
   Callee-saved registers that are used are saved in the prologue and restored before ret. When call arguments are in argument registers, they
   go through the stack (writing them in order would clobber them)

Also: if an `icmp` value is used only by `brif`, it becomes `cmp` + `jcc`; if nothing is passed to else, jump directly; a `jmp` to the immediately next block is a nop.
Floating point values are placed in xmm8 to xmm15 (clobbered by calls, so only for intervals with no calls), and `fadd` and similar also read the second operand from a register.
Copies between variables and values are direct. When calling our own functions (`_x..`), `al` for variadic arguments is not written.
`MINCLIF_NO_REGALLOC=1` disables allocation (for comparison).

Results:
- Run times from `python3 bench/runtime.py` (driver2 -O. All outputs match):

  | | no allocation | integers only | + floating point, direct copies | Cranelift path (`zustc -O`) | rustc -O |
  |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
  | fib | 111 ms | 90 | 96 | 82 | 30 |
  | hashmap | 341 | 210 | 208 | 149 | 103 |
  | matmul | 242 | 190 | 158 | 91 | 45 |
  | nbody | 1150 | 725 | 516 | 83 | 47 |
  | sieve | 346 | 185 | 169 | 141 | 109 |
  | sort | 624 | 344 | 341 | 252 | 210 |
  | strings | 227 | 119 | 120 | 70 | 42 |

  All are faster than rustc's debug build, and the build takes about half the time of the Cranelift path. Execution has not yet caught up with the Cranelift path
  (struct fields and array elements stay in memory, and instruction selection is still simple)
- A simple loop (sum of 1000 elements × 200 thousand times): 1.08 seconds → 0.44 seconds (the same as rustc opt-level=0)
- Time for the self-hosted compiler to compile itself: 18.0 seconds → **10.1 seconds** (front 3.2 → 1.7 seconds, codegen 13.0 → 7.6 seconds).
  The compiler executable went from 23 MB → 12 MB
- Added wild (0.10) as the linker (`cargo install --locked wild-linker --version 0.10.0`. link.rs uses wild > mold > ld.lld in that order).
  Workspace benchmark: cold 355 ms, function body change 37 ms, bin change 60 ms

   後ろ向きのデータフロー (区間の入口・出口で生きているか) で生きている区間の端まで延ばした範囲を生存区間にし、線形走査で
   rbx・r12〜r15 (呼ばれた側が保存: 呼び出しをまたぐ区間用) と rsi・rdi・r8〜r10 (呼び出しを含まない区間用) に割り当てる。
   足りなければ「読み書きの回数 / 長さ」が小さいものをスロットへ。浮動小数点・i128・スロットを直接使う値 (アドレスとして
   使う・幅の違う読み書き) はスロットのまま。すぐ後が trap の呼び出し (panic) は戻らないので、またぐとしない
3. **本番**: 割り当てを持った Emitter で記録した命令をもう一度組み立てる。今までの命令の組み立てはそのまま使え、
   値の読み書き (load_rax / store_rax など) が割り当てを見る。よく使う命令はレジスタの形で書く: 64 / 32 bit の
   add / sub / and / or / xor / imul と cmp は `mov d, a; op d, b`、定数は直接、load / store は `[base + off]`。
   使った呼ばれた側が保存するレジスタはプロローグで保存し ret の前に戻す。呼び出しの引数が引数のレジスタにあるときは
   スタックを経由する (順に書くと壊れる)

あわせて: `icmp` の値を `brif` だけが使うなら `cmp` + `jcc` にする、else に渡すものがなければ直接飛ぶ、すぐ次への `jmp` は nop。
浮動小数点は xmm8〜15 (呼び出しで壊れるので、呼び出しを含まない区間だけ) に置き、`fadd` などは 2 つ目もレジスタから読む。
変数と値の間は直接写す。自分の関数 (`_x..`) を呼ぶときは可変長引数用の `al` を書かない。
`MINCLIF_NO_REGALLOC=1` で割り当てなし (比較用)。

  | sort | 624 | 344 | 341 | 252 | 210 |

# Placing fields of stack structs in registers (minclif)

Date: 2026-11-16

- The addresses of slots (temporary areas for structs, tuples, arrays) are tracked during analysis: a `stack_addr` value, and that value plus a constant, are
  "(slot, offset)". If that address is used only by load / store / constant addition (passing it to a call, storing it, or
  using it in other computations counts as escaping), reads and writes do not overlap, and the same location always has the same type, then each (slot, offset)
  field becomes one variable (scalar replacement). Allocation treats them like values and variables, and fields that could not be placed in a register
  use their location in the slot. The address value is not created
- acg's struct copy changed from 8 bytes at a time to field by field (with each field's type) (so that read and write widths line up with the fields)
- Slots zeroed at entry (drop flags) are not turned into variables. `MINCLIF_NO_SROA=1` turns this off
- A loop over a struct passed by value and returned by value (the same as tests/acg/struct_fields_regs.rs, 20 million times): 176 ms → 147 ms (rustc -O 87 ms).
  bench/rt barely changes (the structs in nbody and others are inside a Vec: on the heap)
- The self-hosted compiler compiling itself: 9.7 seconds

Upgraded Rust to 1.100.0 and wild to 0.11.0 (`rustup update stable`, `cargo install --locked wild-linker`).

reference.quote:
# A Cranelift backend for driver2 (compared with minclif)

Date: 2026-11-16

minclif's FunctionBuilder records every instruction acg calls as an `Op`. We added a backend that rebuilds that sequence as Cranelift IR and
compiles it (`src/clif_backend.rs`, `ZUSTC_BACKEND=cranelift`). acg, inlining, the cache and .o
writing are shared, so only the backend is compared, with the same frontend and the same instruction sequence.

- Values map minclif value numbers → Cranelift values. Blocks, variables, slots and functions are also mapped by number (recording now also keeps
  each instruction's return value). acg sometimes uses a value in a block that the value does not dominate (no problem for minclif, which keeps values in slots), so
  values used in a segment other than their definition's become Cranelift Variables, and cranelift_frontend builds the SSA
- Drop-flag slots are created midway, so after building, 0 is written at the start of the entry block
- Relocations are returned by name (calls are PLT32, symbols are GOTPCREL). Trap codes are also the same as minclif's
- `tests/driver2_cranelift.rs`: builds probe / examples / acg without -O and with -O, and checks that output, stderr and exit code are the same as minclif (all match).
  The self-hosted compiler built with Cranelift also emits the same .o as the one built with minclif

Run times (`python3 bench/runtime.py`, ms):

| | driver2 -O (minclif) | driver2 + Cranelift | driver2 + Cranelift -O | previous Cranelift path (`zustc -O`) | rustc -O |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| fib | 110 | 91 | 79 | 79 | 31 |
| hashmap | 214 | 155 | 144 | 148 | 112 |
| matmul | 168 | 105 | 76 | 85 | 40 |
| nbody | 522 | 232 | 86 | 105 | 54 |
| sieve | 158 | 150 | 154 | 134 | 94 |
| sort | 334 | 294 | 233 | 248 | 208 |
| strings | 111 | 91 | 68 | 73 | 42 |

Compared on the self-hosted compiler (about 33 thousand lines):

| Backend | Compiling it (-j 1, including acg) | Resulting executable | Time for the resulting compiler to compile itself |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| minclif | 2.40 seconds | 8.8 MB | 11.5 seconds |
| minclif -O | 3.15 seconds | 10.6 MB | 10.1 seconds |
| Cranelift (opt none) | 5.07 seconds | 5.4 MB | 6.9 seconds |
| Cranelift -O (speed, backtracking) | 8.26 seconds | 6.6 MB | **6.0 seconds** |
| Cranelift -O (speed, single_pass) | 6.95 seconds | 9.2 MB | 8.9 seconds |

(The compiler built with rustc -O takes 1.6 seconds.) The workspace benchmark (`bench/ws_bench.py`) with minclif / Cranelift: cold 440 / 727 ms,
no changes 7 / 6 ms, function body change 42 / 36 ms, bin change 74 / 67 ms (with the per-function cache, compilation after a change is small).

What we learned: minclif compiles about 2 times faster than Cranelift (opt none), and about 2.6 times faster when both use -O, but the code it emits is 1.0 to 6 times slower
(1.7 times for the self-hosted compiler). Incremental builds compile only the changed functions, so the difference in compile speed
only matters for cold builds.

At this point, the modules that do not depend on external crates (lexer / enc / fxhash / prelude / link / testgen / program / ast_consteval / solver / ctors / ast_infer / minclif / ast_codegen), and
those with small dependencies for which we could write replacements (elfz: zstd, macros: proc_macro2), can be compiled with zustc and give the same results as rustc.
The rest, front (lookups that walk the syn syntax tree) / infer (the syn version; ast_infer, the version for our own syntax tree, exists) / consteval (constant promotion in codegen) / closure / codegen / driver / cache, is written on top of syn and cranelift.
The replacement for syn will be moved over starting from front, built on src/parse.rs (our own syntax tree). The replacement for cranelift (our own code generation) comes after that.

# Building small real-world crates (`cratebench/`)

Date: 2026-11-16

The sources of small crates from crates.io are placed as-is in `cratebench/vendor/` (licenses included), and built as a workspace together with an app that uses them
(`cratebench/apps/<name>/main.rs`). `python3 cratebench/run.py [names..]` compares with
rustc (the lib as an rlib with `--extern`): whether the output is the same as rustc -O, build time (cold / noop / one edit in the app),
run time and size. The targets are in `cratebench/crates.txt` (name, edition, features).

Added:
- Evaluation of `#[cfg(..)]` / `#[cfg_attr(..)]` / `cfg!(..)` (`crates/syntax/src/cfg.rs`. Features come from the workspace's `features=a,b`
  or `--features=`. Values for x86-64 Linux; `debug_assertions` is true unless -O). `extern crate x;` is removed
- Macro calls in item position are also expanded inside `mod` / `impl` / `trait`. `$x:expr` stops at the end of an expression (`$($len:expr)+`)
- Constant expressions: associated consts in impls (`i128::MAX_STR_LEN`), integer methods such as `u128::MAX.ilog10()`. `const _: () = ..;` is skipped
- prelude: `chunks_exact` (`remainder`), `Read` / `BufRead` (implementations for `&[u8]`), `ExactSizeIterator`, `slice::Iter::len`
- Methods and bounds of `impl Tr for &[u8]`, built-in `AsRef<str>` / `AsRef<[T]>` (the target of `as_ref()` comes from the expected type or the function's bounds),
  `FromIterator` bounds, closures inside blanket impls, `&mut [u8; N] as &mut [u8]`, `&u8 >> 4`
- `?` inside closures: the error type of the returned Result is taken from the `?`
- When impls with the same name are lined up per array length (`impl FromHex for [u8; 1]` .. `[u8; 4096]`), the one whose self type matches is chosen
- A type alias name that starts with a lowercase letter because of the crate prefix (`fnv__FnvHashMap`) is no longer skipped as a module
- Bugs fixed: the `&&str` → `&str` deref coercion loaded a fat pointer (corrupting the value). For a let without annotation where
  the type from type inference differs from the actual type, a coercion is tried, and if that fails the actual type is used

# Multiple crates with many dependencies (`bench/deps_bench.py`)

Date: 2026-11-16

The leaves are 6 real crates from cratebench; above them are N generated intermediate crates (a DAG where each depends on 2 to 3 real crates and on up to 3
previous intermediate crates, using structs, traits, generic functions, closures and cfg_if!); an app sits at the top. We compare with cargo
(a workspace with path dependencies, dev profile, 4 parallel jobs). The scenarios are cold / noop / changing the body of a function in the bottom intermediate crate m0
(low-body) / changing the signature of a pub function in m0 (low-sig, users fixed too) / changing the app. We check that the output is the same as cargo's.

At first, each user crate re-expanded and re-analyzed the whole source of its transitive dependencies every time, so as dependencies grew, cargo caught up in cold and low-sig
(with 100 crates, cold 3718 ms (cargo 3250), low-sig 1581 ms (cargo 1578). Of the analysis, macro expansion took 1.5 seconds). What we fixed:
- Macro expansion of dependency crates happens once: each crate expands only its own part, with just the macro definitions of its dependency crates attached
- What is passed to users is the interface (`crates/syntax/src/stub.rs`): bodies of non-generic functions become `{ loop {} }` (the dependency
  crate compiles them itself). Generic functions, generic impls, traits, `const fn`, `-> impl Trait` and `async fn` are kept.
  The expansion and the interface are saved in `<name>.prep`. `ZUSTC_NO_DEP_STUB=1` gives the old behavior
- Cache entries (item summaries, function machine code) created by child processes building in parallel are returned to the parent, and crates in later groups inherit them through fork
  (monomorphization of the prelude and item summaries of dependency crates' items are the same across many crates: functions compiled in a 100-crate cold build went 11360 → 5984)
- Fine-grained fingerprint (`<name>.fp2`): only the hashes of the dependency crates' interface items reachable by name from the crate's own identifiers
  (impls are reached through the header's type and trait names, methods by name: errs on the side of including too much rather than missing something). Even if the old fingerprint
  differs, nothing is rebuilt if the fine-grained fingerprint is the same. Since bodies are removed, signatures of functions in dependencies of dependencies do not reach users
- With bodies removed, methods are no longer reached by name when the crate's own type is made into a `Box<dyn Tr>`: they are also compiled from vtable entries

- What is passed to users is only the items of the dependency crates' interfaces that are reachable by name from the crate (the same traversal as the fine-grained fingerprint).
  Everything else is blanked out (`use` is kept because it is needed for name resolution). This way, flattening, item summary, Program and prelude selection cover only what is used
  (for m50 with 100 crates, dependency items went from around 800 → 150). `ZUSTC_NO_DEP_PRUNE=1` turns it off.
  An impl's names are the trait and type names in its header; the inside of `impl<..>`, everything from `where` on, and primitive types are not counted, and trait implementations
  for std types (`Vec`, etc.) are reached by the trait name alone (`impl FromHex for [u8; 4]` was reachable from every crate that wrote `u8`)

Results (ms, median. "Before" is before reuse, "Middle" is up to interfaces, fingerprints and cache sharing, the right column is after restricting to what is reachable by name):

| Intermediate crates | Scenario | zustc before | zustc middle | zustc | cargo |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 20 (400 functions) | cold | 759 | 462 | 261 | 858 |
| | low-body | 29 | 33 | 23 | 373 |
| | low-sig | 249 | 54 | 32 | 398 |
| | app-body | 62 | 42 | 24 | 113 |
| 50 (1500 functions) | cold | 1927 | 1050 | 612 | 1719 |
| | low-body | 33 | 39 | 27 | 797 |
| | low-sig | 731 | 76 | 61 | 803 |
| | app-body | 110 | 72 | 34 | 164 |
| 100 (3000 functions) | cold | 3718 | 1866 | 1190 | 2933 |
| | noop | 11 | 13 | 11 | 119 |
| | low-body | 46 | 42 | 33 | 1434 |
| | low-sig | 1581 | 126 | 87 | 1465 |
| | app-body | 204 | 107 | 49 | 246 |

After that, we made the machine code of prelude functions reused across crates (functions compiled in a 100-crate cold build went 5984 → 4973):
- The key of a closed prelude function (its body is in the prelude, it is non-generic or its type arguments are only prelude or primitive types, and it is not a closure) is
  only the compiler ID, the body, its own signature and `#[panic_handler]`. Signatures of referenced items were collected generously by the last segment of the name, so
  the user's `Acc5::push` got into the key of prelude functions that call `.push(`, making the key differ per crate
- Panic locations of prelude functions are lines inside the prelude (from `PRELUDE_LINE` = 49152 onward, the location table maps lines to the file `<zustc prelude>`).
  Selected prelude items are placed at their original lines (with newlines in between). Before, the base line for prelude locations changed with the length of the user's source and
  with the prelude selection, so the cache missed, and the output showed meaningless locations such as `src/main.rs:259`
- Instances of dependency crates' generic functions are also reused: for a function whose body is in the prelude or in dependency crate j and whose type arguments do not
  include this crate's types (a closed function), the key includes only the referenced items within "crates visible from j and from the crates of the type arguments' types". Panic locations
  are kept as lines within j's text: the trap table adds the position on the user side when the .o is written, and for locations passed as constants (index checks, assert_eq!,
  unwrap callers) j's tag (`crate_tag`) goes into the upper bits of the line, and at run time j's table is selected from the list of dependency crates' tables in the executable's table (`_xT__exe`)
  and looked up. As a side effect, this also fixed the lookup of constant-passed locations inside dependency crates through the executable's table
  (which had printed a different file and line). Added an out-of-range index inside a dependency crate's generic function to tests/workspace.
  In this benchmark there were only about 80 duplicates, so the cold time is within measurement noise (1088 to 1223 ms with 100 crates)
- We decided not to split Program into "dependency base + own items": measured, the Program stage is about 1 ms per crate
  (4% of the cold total, 2% of an app change), and the base (the reachable part of dependencies and the selected prelude) also differs per crate and cannot be shared

| Intermediate crates | Scenario | zustc | cargo |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| 20 | cold | 265 | 862 |
| 50 | cold | 553 | 1731 |
| 100 | cold | 1088 | 3070 |
| 100 | noop / low-body / low-sig / app-body | 11 / 37 / 94 / 49 | 120 / 1481 / 1557 / 250 |

When a dependency crate changes (even just a body), cargo recompiles all its users. zustc, with its per-function cache and
interface fingerprints, rebuilds only the crates that use what changed. Remaining: each crate rebuilds the item summaries and
Program for the prelude (a little over 500 items) (the selected prelude differs per crate, so the whole Program is not shared). Most of the remaining cold time is function
compilation (Cranelift).

葉に cratebench の実在のクレート 6 個、その上に生成した中間クレート N 個 (それぞれ実在のクレート 2〜3 個と前の中間クレート
最大 3 個に依存する DAG。struct・trait・総称関数・クロージャ・cfg_if! を使う)、いちばん上に app を置き、cargo
(path 依存のワークスペース、dev プロファイル、4 並列) と比べる。場面は cold / noop / いちばん下の中間クレート m0 の関数の
本体の変更 (low-body) / m0 の pub 関数のシグネチャの変更 (low-sig、使う側も直す) / app の変更。出力は cargo と同じか確かめる。

最初は、使う側のクレートが推移的な依存のソース全体を毎回展開・解析し直していたので、依存が増えると cold と low-sig で cargo に
並ばれた (100 クレートで cold 3718 ms (cargo 3250)、low-sig 1581 ms (cargo 1578)。解析の内訳はマクロの展開が 1.5 秒)。直したもの:

- 使う側に渡すのはインターフェース (`crates/syntax/src/stub.rs`): 総称でない関数の本体を `{ loop {} }` にする (依存する
  クレート自身がコンパイルする)。総称関数・総称な impl・trait・`const fn`・`-> impl Trait`・`async fn` は残す。
  展開とインターフェースは `<名前>.prep` に保存する。`ZUSTC_NO_DEP_STUB=1` で前の動き

  (prelude の単相化や依存するクレートのアイテムの要約は多くのクレートで同じ: 100 クレートの cold でコンパイルする関数 11360 → 5984)
- 細かい指紋 (`<名前>.fp2`): 依存するクレートのインターフェースのアイテムのうち、自分の識別子から名前でたどって届くもの

  違っても細かい指紋が同じなら作り直さない。本体を消してあるので、依存の依存の関数のシグネチャは使う側に届かない

| 中間クレート | 場面 | zustc 前 | zustc 中 | zustc | cargo |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 20 (400 関数) | cold | 759 | 462 | 261 | 858 |
| | low-body | 29 | 33 | 23 | 373 |
| | low-sig | 249 | 54 | 32 | 398 |

| 50 (1500 関数) | cold | 1927 | 1050 | 612 | 1719 |
| | low-body | 33 | 39 | 27 | 797 |
| | low-sig | 731 | 76 | 61 | 803 |
| | app-body | 110 | 72 | 34 | 164 |
| 100 (3000 関数) | cold | 3718 | 1866 | 1190 | 2933 |
| | noop | 11 | 13 | 11 | 119 |
| | low-body | 46 | 42 | 33 | 1434 |
| | low-sig | 1581 | 126 | 87 | 1465 |
| | app-body | 204 | 107 | 49 | 246 |

- 閉じた prelude の関数 (本体が prelude で、総称でないか型引数が prelude・プリミティブの型だけ、クロージャでない) のキーは、
  コンパイラ ID・本体・自分のシグネチャ・`#[panic_handler]` だけにする。参照先のシグネチャを名前の最後で多めに取っていたので、
  `.push(` を呼ぶ prelude の関数のキーにユーザの `Acc5::push` が入り、クレートごとに違うキーになっていた
